unit.title: Perform manual metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Low carbon steel pipe)

summary: This unit is about welding low carbon steel pipe with manual metal arc welding (MMAW) to an AWS code and a written welding procedure specification (WPS). You will learn to read pipe sizes, fittings and isometric drawings; prepare, fit up and tack pipe joints; run an E6010 open root, a hot pass and E7018 fill and cap passes in the rolled and fixed positions; and inspect, test and record the work while leading a small pipe crew.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It takes the stick welding you learned on plate and applies it to **low carbon steel pipe**, welded to the **AWS code the Centre uses** and to a **welding procedure specification (WPS)**. Pipe carries water, steam, air, fuel and chemicals under pressure, so a pipe weld must be sound all the way through, not just neat on the outside.

Pipe welding is harder than plate welding for three reasons. The joint curves, so your position, your electrode angle and gravity change all the way round. The root is welded from one side only, so you cannot see or reach the inside. And many pipe welds are inspected by radiography, which shows faults that look fine from outside.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees who can already weld plate in all positions with MMAW, and who will now plan, weld, inspect and lead pipe work in Jamaican workshops, plants, hotels, farms and on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the code and the WPS
Find the WPS for each joint, check that it covers the pipe, wall, position and electrodes, and check that each welder is qualified for the work.
Read pipe sizes, fittings and drawings
Understand nominal pipe size, schedule and wall thickness, fittings and flanges, and work out cut lengths from an isometric drawing.
Control the hazards of heavy rolling pipe, trenches, site work, fume, fire, electric shock and radiography.
Prepare and fit up pipe joints
Cut, bevel and clean pipe ends; set the root face, root gap and alignment; tack the joint so it stays true.
Weld the root and hot pass
Run an open root with E6010 using a keyhole, then a hot pass to clean and strengthen it.
Weld the fill and cap in each position
Lay E7018 fill and cap passes in the 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G positions, cleaning between passes.
Inspect pipe welds by eye and with gauges, prepare and judge bend tests, and understand radiography and pressure tests.
Lead the crew and keep records
Plan the work, control electrodes and quality, do the calculations, keep the weld log and report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on pipe sizes, the WPS, positions, safety, preparation, electrodes, technique, defects, testing, qualification, drawings and calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms and simple sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practicals**: an open-root pipe butt joint in the 2G position (E6010 root, hot pass, E7018 fill and cap) with fit-up records, inspection and bend tests; and a small pipe spool with a weld neck flange and an elbow, built from an isometric drawing with a cut list and a weld log.

blocks.note: At Level 3 the assessor wants to hear **why** you do each step, not only what you do. When you learn a rule in this kit, learn its reason too.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Codes, the WPS and welder qualification

blocks.p: Pipe work for a client is usually welded "to the AWS code the Centre uses" or to another named code. The code sets the rules: how procedures and welders are qualified, how welds are inspected, and what faults are allowed. On the job, you meet the code mainly through three documents.

head: Document
What it is
Who uses it
rows: The written recipe for a joint: what to weld, with what, and how.
The welder at the joint; the team leader checking the work.
The record of a test joint welded to prove the WPS works: the real settings used and the test results.
The engineer or inspector who approves the WPS.
**WPQ** (welder performance qualification), often called the welder's test certificate
Proof that a named welder passed a test, and the range of work that test covers.
The team leader giving out work; the client's inspector.

blocks.h: What a pipe WPS tells you

head: Item
Example for a carbon steel pipe butt joint
rows: Low carbon steel pipe, for example ASTM A106 or A53 Grade B, or API 5L Grade B
For example 60–220 mm outside diameter, 3–12 mm wall
Single-V butt, bevel 37.5° each side (75° included), root face 1–2 mm, root gap 2.5–3.2 mm, open root, no backing
Root: E6010, 3.2 mm. Hot pass: E6010 or E7018. Fill and cap: E7018, 2.5 or 3.2 mm
DC electrode positive (DCEP); an amp range for each electrode and pass
For example a minimum of 10 °C and dry metal; more for thick walls
Stringer or weave, maximum weave width, cleaning between passes
Visual on every weld; radiography of a stated percentage of joints

blocks.p: A WPS covers a **range**: a range of wall thickness, diameter, positions and electrodes. If the job falls outside that range, the WPS does not apply. You do not stretch it; you ask for a WPS that covers the job.

blocks.note: Some changes are so important that they need a new procedure test. Changing the electrode group or the base metal group, going outside the thickness range, or adding or removing heat treatment are typical examples. That is why a welder must never change the WPS on his own, even when he is sure his way works.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A welder qualifies by welding a test coupon to a WPS, watched by an inspector. The coupon is inspected and then bend tested or radiographed. If it passes, the WPQ lists the **positions**, **diameters**, **wall thicknesses** and **electrode groups** the welder may weld. A test does not cover everything: it covers what the code's tables say it covers.

head: Pipe test position
How the pipe is held
Groove positions generally covered
rows: Axis horizontal; the pipe is rolled so you weld on top
Axis vertical; the weld runs round horizontally
Axis horizontal and fixed; you weld up each side
6G with a restriction ring fitted close to the joint
All positions, and the branch (T, K and Y) connections the code names

ul: **Pipe and plate:** a pipe test generally also covers plate, but a plate test covers pipe only above a large diameter that the code sets. On pipe the position changes all the way round the joint, which a plate test never shows.
**Size limits:** a test on small pipe covers only a band of diameters, and a test wall covers only a band of thicknesses. Read the code's table before you give out joints.
**Continuity:** a qualification lapses if the welder does not use the process for too long, often six months. Keep a continuity log for each welder.
**Traceability:** the assessor marks each test coupon with the welder's number before welding starts, so coupons cannot be swapped and each result is traced to one person.

blocks.note: Before you give a welder a joint, check three things: is there a WPS for this joint, does the welder's WPQ cover its position, diameter and wall, and is the qualification still in date?
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Carbon steel pipe is ordered by **nominal pipe size (NPS)** in inches, or by **DN** (diameter nominal) in metric. The nominal size is a name, not a measurement. For each size the **outside diameter (OD) stays the same** whatever the wall thickness, so all fittings of that size fit the pipe. The wall thickness is set by the **schedule**: the higher the schedule number, the thicker the wall and the smaller the bore.

Up to NPS 12 the outside diameter is larger than the nominal size; from NPS 14 up, the OD in inches equals the NPS. "Standard" (STD) and "extra strong" (XS) are older names that match schedule 40 and 80 in the common small sizes.

blocks.note: **Bore (inside diameter) = OD − 2 × wall.** For NPS 6 schedule 80: 168.3 − (2 × 10.97) = 168.3 − 21.94 = **146.36 mm**. Always take the OD and wall from the pipe table or the pipe markings, not from the nominal size.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Pipe is marked along its length with the standard and grade (for example A106 B), the size and schedule, and a **heat number** that links it to the steel maker's **mill certificate**. Check the markings against the drawing and the WPS before you cut.

head: Fitting
What it does
Points to know
rows: Centre-line radius = 1.5 × the NPS in inches; for NPS 4 that is 6 in, about 152 mm. Smoother flow, so it is the usual choice.
Turns the run through 90° in less space
Radius = 1 × NPS (about 102 mm for NPS 4). Used only where space is tight.
For NPS 4 LR, centre-to-end about 64 mm
Centre-to-end from the fitting table (about 105 mm for NPS 4)
An eccentric reducer keeps one side flat (for example the top of a pump suction)
Closes the end of a run

head: Flange
How it is welded
Typical use
rows: **Butt welded** to the pipe through its long tapered hub; the joint can be radiographed
Pressure, heat and heavy duty lines
The pipe slides inside; **fillet welded** inside and outside
Lower pressure water and air lines; easier to fit
The pipe sits in a socket; one outside fillet
No hole; bolted to close a line
Ends of lines and test points

blocks.p: Flanges are made in **pressure classes** (for example 150, 300, 600). Check the class, the size and the face type (often raised face) against the drawing. Protect the machined face from spatter and arc strikes: a damaged face will leak.

blocks.note: Unless the drawing says otherwise, flange bolt holes are set to **straddle** the vertical and horizontal centre lines ("two-holed"), so that a flange at the other end of the line will match. Check it with a level across two holes before tacking.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Socket weld joints on small bore

blocks.p: On a socket weld, push the pipe into the socket until it touches the bottom, then **pull it back about 1.5 mm** before tacking. The gap lets the pipe expand as the fillet is welded and stops the weld shrinkage cracking the root of the fillet.

Pipe runs are drawn as **isometrics**: a single-line 3-D view with the three directions drawn at set angles. An isometric shows the route, the dimensions (usually centre to centre or face to centre, in millimetres), every fitting and flange, the flow direction, a north arrow, the **weld numbers**, where the run is split into **spools** (pieces made in the shop) and which welds are **field welds** made on site. The title block gives the line number, size, material, schedule and drawing revision.
The drawing gives centre-to-centre or face-to-centre dimensions. The pipe is shorter, because the fittings take up part of that length and each joint has a root gap.

blocks.note: **Cut length = dimension on the drawing − the length each fitting takes − the root gaps.** Example: two NPS 4 LR elbows, 1 200 mm centre to centre, root gap 3 mm. Each elbow takes 152 mm, and there are two gaps. Cut length = 1 200 − 152 − 152 − 3 − 3 = **890 mm**. For a weld neck flange, take off its length through the hub from the flange table (about 76 mm for an NPS 4 class 150 flange).
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Write every cut length on a **cut list**, with the line and spool number, the pipe size and schedule and the heat number. Mark each piece with paint marker as it is cut. Check the sum against the drawing before you cut the next piece.

Pipe work adds its own hazards to those of arc welding: heavy round pieces that roll, work in trenches and on sites, lines that held fuel, long hours in hot weather and, on some jobs, radiography. As team leader you must spot these hazards before work starts and put the controls in place.

head: Hazard
What can happen
Controls
rows: Pipe rolls off racks, trestles or trucks and crushes feet, legs or hands
Chock or wedge pipe on racks and stands
Keep hands out of pinch points when pipe is rolled or lowered
Use slings and lifting gear rated for the load; team lifts for heavy pieces
The sides collapse and bury the welder; people or spoil fall in; fumes and gas collect in the bottom
Trench shored, sloped or boxed as a competent person decides
Spoil and machines kept back from the edge
A ladder or ramp to get in and out
Fumes extracted or blown clear; someone watching from the top
Lines that held fuel, oil or gas
Vapour left inside explodes when heated
Never cut or weld until a competent person has cleaned, gas-freed and tested the line
Hot-work permit where the site uses one
Rain, sweat, wet ground and kneeling on pipe put you in the circuit
Dry gloves and clothing; dry mat or board
Machine out of the rain; stop work in rain
Arc eye and skin burns to the welder and to people passing on site
Helmet with the right shade, all skin covered
Screens round the joint on site
Fume collects in trenches, pits and inside large pipes
Coatings removed from the weld area
Sparks land in dry grass, rubbish, cardboard or inside buildings
Clear or cover anything that burns
Fire watch during and after the work
Thin cut-off discs shatter; sparks and chips hit eyes and face
Disc rated for the grinder's speed, not cracked, guard on
Dizziness, cramps, confusion and collapse when working long hours in the sun or inside hot pipe
Water at hand, shade and rest breaks

blocks.note: Site pipe work in Jamaica is often done near the sea, in the rainy seasons (roughly May to June and September to November) or in full sun. Plan screens against wind and rain, shade for the crew, dry boards to stand on, and time to stop when the weather turns. Keep the welding machine (often an engine-driven welder on site) out of puddles and away from the trench edge.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Pipe welds are often checked by **radiography (RT)** with X-rays or a gamma-ray source. The rays cannot be seen or felt, and they harm the body. Only **licensed, trained radiographers** may do it, under Jamaica's radiation safety law. When they work, they set up a barrier and warning signs round a controlled area.

ul: Stop work and move out of the controlled area when the radiographer says, and stay out until they say it is clear.
Never cross a radiography barrier or move its signs, even "just for a minute".
Plan radiography for times when few people are about, such as the end of the shift.

blocks.p: Most carbon steel pipe welded with MMAW uses two kinds of electrode: a **cellulosic** electrode (E6010) for the open root and often the hot pass, and a **low-hydrogen** electrode (E7018) for the fill and cap. The WPS names the electrodes; you must know why they were chosen.

head: Electrode
Coating and current
Why it is used on pipe
Storage
rows: Cellulosic (high in cellulose); DC electrode positive only
Forceful, deep-digging arc that melts through the root faces
Thin, fast-freezing slag, so it works in every position
Good for open roots and hot passes
Sealed tin at normal room temperature, kept dry
**Never bake it**: the coating needs a little moisture to work, and baking ruins it
Cellulosic; AC or DC electrode positive
Like E6010 but runs on AC; used where only an AC machine is available and the WPS allows it
Low hydrogen with iron powder; AC or DC electrode positive
Tough, crack-resistant weld metal with very little hydrogen
Sealed packet, then a **holding oven** (often about 120–150 °C) once opened
On the job, a few at a time in a **heated quiver**
Re-dry as the maker says if exposed too long

blocks.p: Why change electrodes after the root? The E6010 root is quick and reliable, but its gas shield is rich in hydrogen. The fill and cap make up most of the joint, so they are laid with E7018, whose weld metal is tough and low in hydrogen and less likely to crack. That is why a WPS with an E6010 root still calls for E7018 everywhere else.

blocks.note: Codes limit how long low-hydrogen electrodes may be out of the oven or quiver, often about 4 hours for E7018. Electrodes past the limit go back for re-drying exactly as the maker says, or are scrapped. Never mix E6010 and E7018 in one quiver or oven: they need opposite care.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: These are typical figures only. The WPS gives the range for each pass, and the electrode maker gives a range on the packet. Set within both, test on scrap pipe, and follow your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Pipe is welded on a **DC** machine (rectifier, inverter or engine-driven welder) with the electrode lead on **positive** (DCEP) for E6010 and E7018.
A cellulosic root needs a machine with enough open-circuit voltage and arc force; many inverters have a cellulosic or pipe setting.
A **remote current control** at the joint lets the welder lower the current as the pipe heats up, without walking back to the machine.
Fix the work clamp to clean metal on the pipe close to the joint. On long or magnetised pipe, where you place the clamp affects arc blow.

blocks.p: Pipe that has been lifted with magnets, or long welded lines, can be magnetised, especially near open ends. On DC the magnetism pushes the arc to one side, so the root will not fuse evenly. To control it: move the work clamp, or wrap the work lead a few turns round the pipe near the joint; weld towards a heavy tack; hold a shorter arc and angle the electrode against the blow; lower the current a little. Changing to AC needs an AC electrode (such as E6011) and a WPS that allows it.
Most root faults start at fit-up. A good welder cannot make a sound root on a bad bevel, a wrong gap or ends that do not line up, so the WPS sets the preparation exactly.

head: Feature
Typical figure (follow the WPS)
What it controls
rows: 37.5° on each pipe end (75° included); some WPS use 30° (60° included)
Room for the electrode to reach the root and fuse the side walls
Too thick: lack of penetration. Too thin or none: burn-through and icicles
Too small: lack of penetration. Too wide: burn-through, icicles and a slow, hot root
A step inside the bore leaves one root face unfused and raises stress

blocks.note: The **root face and the root gap work together**. A thick root face needs a wider gap or more current to fuse through; a thin root face with a wide gap falls through. That is why the WPS sets both, and why you check both all round the joint.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Cut pipe square with a pipe saw, band saw, abrasive cut-off saw or a wheel pipe cutter. Check the end is square with a wrap-round (a strip of card or thin sheet wrapped round the pipe as a guide).

Bevel by machine (a pipe bevelling machine or end-prep tool), or with an oxy-fuel torch on a band or track, then **grind** the bevel to bright metal. Torch-cut bevels carry oxide and slag that cause porosity and lack of fusion.
Grind the root face flat and even with a file or grinder.
Clean the bevel and about **25 mm inside and outside** to bright metal: no rust, mill scale, paint, oil or coating.
Check the bevel angle with a **bevel protractor or pipe bevel gauge**, and the root face with a rule or gauge.

flow: Check the WPS, and the pipe size, schedule and heat number
Set both pipes on stands or rollers, at a working height, in line
Bring the ends together in a line-up clamp (or with a straight edge laid across at four points round the pipe)
Set the root gap with a spacer of the right size, such as the bare end of an electrode, or a gap gauge
Check the inside alignment all round with a hi-lo gauge; turn one pipe to find the best match if the ends are slightly out of round
Tack, then re-check the gap and alignment before welding

ul: Tack in the root with the root electrode (E6010), with the same care as the root itself: each tack fully penetrated and fused.
On small pipe, put three or four tacks evenly round the joint. On a 5G joint welded uphill, keep tacks away from **6 o'clock**, where the root starts, and often from 12 o'clock, where it finishes.
Grind each end of every tack to a **feather edge** (a thin taper) so the root runs smoothly into and out of it.
Some jobs use **bridge tacks**: small bars or pieces welded across the outside of the joint, so the root runs clear of tacks. They are ground off as the root reaches them, and the spots checked.
A tack that cracks when the clamp is removed, or as the joint cools, is **ground out completely** and re-made. Never weld over a cracked tack: the crack stays in the root.

blocks.note: When a tight gap must be opened slightly, a **thin cut-off disc** run carefully through the root opens it evenly. Do not hammer a joint open after tacking: the tacks crack.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Positions round a pipe are named like a clock seen from one end: **12 o'clock** is the top, **6 o'clock** the bottom, 3 and 9 o'clock the sides. Use clock positions on fit-up records, inspection reports and when you tell a welder where a fault is.

sections.title: Welding the joint: root, hot pass, fill and cap

head: Pass
Its job
Usual electrode
rows: Fuses both root faces and forms an even bead inside the bore
Laid soon after the root at a higher current; melts out slag trapped along the root's edges and thickens the root so later passes do not burn through it
E6010, or E7018 after the root has been ground (as the WPS says)
Build up the groove with sound, low-hydrogen metal fused into both side walls
Finishes the joint just above the pipe surface, lapping a little over each bevel edge, with no undercut

flow: Strike on the bevel or on a feathered tack just past 6 o'clock, and move into the gap
Push the arc into the gap until a small **keyhole** opens at the front of the pool: both root faces are melting through
Use a **whip and pause**: flick the arc a few millimetres forward and up to let the pool freeze, then bring it back and hold it briefly to fill the keyhole
Keep a short, tight arc, with the electrode nearly square to the pipe; change your wrist and body as you climb so that angle stays the same
Watch the keyhole: keep it the same size all the way up
Stop at a tack or just past 12 o'clock; grind the start and the stop to a taper
Weld the second half from the bottom, tying into the tapered start, and finish over the top

head: What you see
What it means
What to do
rows: The keyhole is growing; drops sag inside
Too much heat at that point
Shorten the pause, travel a little faster, lower the current a little
Too little heat; the root faces are not melting through
Lengthen the pause, push the electrode further into the gap, check the gap ahead
Hollow root inside at 5–7 o'clock (concavity or suck-back)
Gravity pulls the overhead pool back from the inside
Push the electrode well into the gap, keep a very tight arc and a small keyhole
Excess penetration or icicles near 11–1 o'clock
The pipe has heated up and the pool sags into the bore
Lower the current (a remote control helps), shorten the pause, keep the keyhole small

blocks.note: Uphill (vertical-up) welding is used on most plant, building and water pipe and on most tests. Cross-country pipelines are often welded **downhill** with cellulosic electrodes, using a different joint design and technique. Weld only in the direction the WPS gives.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Cleaning the root and the hot pass

blocks.p: An E6010 root usually has a convex bead in the middle and small grooves of slag along both edges, called **wagon tracks**. Clean the root with a power wire brush. If the WPS allows, grind it lightly with a thin disc to flatten a hump and open the tracks. Then run the **hot pass** at a higher current, soon after the root, so its heat melts out any slag left in the tracks and fuses the edges. A root with a high hump and deep tracks that is not ground will trap slag under the hot pass.

ul: Keep a **short arc** (about the core wire diameter or less). A long arc lets air in and causes porosity.
Strike just ahead of where the pass will start, in the groove, then move back to the start: this melts out the porosity that low-hydrogen electrodes can leave at a cold start.
Weave only as wide as the WPS allows (often no wider than about 2½–3 times the core wire diameter); pause at each side wall so it fuses, and cross the middle a little faster.
**Stagger** the starts and stops of each pass, at least about 25 mm apart, so they do not stack up in one place.
Clean every pass with a chipping hammer and a power wire brush; grind any high spot or bad stop before the next pass.
Fill until the groove is about 1–1.5 mm below the pipe surface, with the bevel edges still showing, ready for the cap.
Lay the cap just past each bevel edge (about 1.5 mm), even in width and height, with the height inside the limit the code gives (often no more than about 3 mm).

head: Position
How you weld it
Faults to watch
rows: Weld near the top (about 11 to 1 o'clock), rolling the pipe a little at a time so the pool stays flat
Uneven bead from rolling too far at once; cold restarts
Root with the electrode tipped slightly up; fill and cap as **small stringers stacked from the bottom up**, each overlapping about half of the one below, electrode angled up a little
Sag and undercut at the top edge; slag trapped between stringers
Each pass in two halves, uphill from just past 6 o'clock to just past 12 o'clock; angles change all the way round
Concavity at the bottom; excess penetration at the top; poor tie-ins
Like 5G, but the joint also slopes; often stringers on the upper side and a controlled weave or stringers on the lower side, as the WPS says
Lack of fusion on the upper bevel; sag on the lower side; tie-ins at top and bottom
As 6G, working round the restriction ring
Poor access: lack of fusion and angle errors next to the ring

blocks.note: On site, wind through an open pipe acts like a chimney: it cools the root and blows the gas shield away inside, so the root comes out porous. Cap or plug the far ends of the line while you weld the root, and put a screen round the joint.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Defect
What it looks like
Main causes
Prevention or cure
rows: The root faces are not fused through; a line or slot along the inside
Gap too small or root face too thick
Current too low; travel too fast
A hole melted right through the root
Too much heat; gap too wide
Pause too long; travel too slow
Too much weld metal inside the bore; drops hanging down
Too much heat at one spot
Gap too wide; root face too thin
Lower current as the pipe heats
The inside of the root is hollow, below the bore surface
Overhead part of a fixed joint
Push the electrode into the gap
Slag lines along both edges of the root
Slag trapped at the root toes
Hot pass too cold or missing
Clean and, where allowed, grind the root
Weld metal lying against the bevel without melting into it
Weave not reaching the walls; travel too fast
Slag trapped between stringers or passes
Wind or draught through the bore
Short arc; strike ahead and move back
A groove at the toe of the cap (or inside at the root)
The cap does not reach the pipe surface; bevel edges still showing
Add a fill or cap pass before finishing
The two pipe walls do not line up inside
Turn the pipe for best match; use a clamp; check before tacking
Lines in or beside the weld; burnt spots on the pipe

blocks.p: Every pipe weld is inspected by eye. Use good light, a torch, an **inspection mirror** to see inside where you can reach, and a weld gauge.

ul: Cap: width and height, undercut depth, porosity, cracks, arc strikes, spatter and tie-ins.
Root (where visible): full and even penetration, no concavity, burn-through, icicles or lack of fusion.
The joint: alignment, and the weld number and welder's mark on the pipe beside it.
Record each fault with its **clock position** and size, and whether the weld is accepted, rejected or sent for more testing.

head: Test
What it finds
Notes
rows: Faults inside the weld: lack of root penetration and fusion, slag, porosity, cracks
X-ray or gamma ray; licensed radiographers only; the usual test on pressure pipe
Faults inside, especially lack of fusion in thick walls
Cracks at or just below the surface of steel
Quick check of caps and ground-out repairs
Cracks and pores open to the surface

blocks.p: A weld can look perfect outside and still have lack of root fusion or slag inside. That is why a code or client calls for radiography on a set percentage of welds, or on all of them.

blocks.h: Bend tests on welder test coupons

flow: The coupon first passes visual inspection
Strips are marked across the weld from the places the code sets round the pipe, so that the overhead, vertical and flat parts of a fixed joint are all tested
Strips are cut cold, by saw or machine, never with a torch near the weld
The cap and root are ground or machined **flush** with the pipe along the strip, with the grinding marks running lengthways, and the edges slightly rounded
Each strip is bent in a **guided bend jig** round a former of the size the code gives
The outside of each bend is checked for open defects against the code's limit

ul: **Face bend:** the cap side is on the outside of the bend, so faults near the cap open up.
**Root bend:** the root side is on the outside, so lack of root fusion and penetration open up.
**Side bend:** a strip turned on its side so the whole wall thickness is stretched; used on thicker walls (often from about 10 mm).
The reinforcement is removed so the strip bends evenly and the test stretches the weld itself; a cap or root left standing would make the strain gather at its toes.
Many codes reject an open defect longer than about 3 mm on the outside of a bend; check the code the Centre uses. A failed strip fails the test, and a retest follows the code's rules.

blocks.p: Finished pipe systems are often **hydrostatically tested**: filled with water, all air vented, and pumped to a test pressure the code gives (often 1.5 times the design pressure), then held while every weld is checked for leaks. Water is used rather than air because water hardly compresses: if a weld fails, the pressure drops at once. Compressed air stores a great deal of energy and can burst a pipe violently. Welds are usually left unpainted until the test is passed.

flow: Mark the defect's position and length from the inspection report
Grind it out completely, checking by eye (and MT or PT if needed) that nothing is left
Shape the excavation so the electrode can reach the bottom
Re-weld to the WPS or the approved repair procedure
Inspect and re-test the repair as the code asks; record it in the weld log

sections.title: Leading the crew: planning, calculations and records

flow: Read the isometrics, the specification and the WPS; check drawing revisions
List every weld with its number on a weld map or weld list
Check each welder's WPQ against the positions, diameters and walls, and give out joints to suit
Check pipe, fittings and electrodes against the drawing and the WPS; set up the electrode oven
Write the cut list and plan the order: roll as many joints as possible in 1G in the shop; leave only closing joints for fixed positions
Plan safety: access, screens, extraction, trench and hot-work controls, radiography times
Set the hold points: fit-up check, root check, final visual, NDT, pressure test
Brief the crew at a toolbox talk, then check and record as the work goes on

ul: **Electrodes:** E7018 in the oven and issued a few at a time in heated quivers; E6010 in sealed tins; types kept apart and labelled.
**Fit-up:** check bevel, root face, gap and alignment on each joint before the root is welded, and record them.
**Watch the root:** check the current and the keyhole, and look at the root before the hot pass.
**Follow the WPS:** no skipped hot passes, no wider gaps "to go faster", no electrode swaps.
**Traceability:** each weld carries its number and the welder's mark, and the details go on the **weld log**: weld number, welder, date, electrodes, passes, inspection and NDT results, repairs.

blocks.note: If a welder or a client asks you to skip a step in the WPS to save time, the answer is no. A WPS step can be changed only by the person responsible for the procedure, in writing, and some changes need a new procedure test.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Sum
How to work it
Example
rows: Length of one pass × number of passes
NPS 6 with 6 passes: 528.8 × 6 = 3 173 mm, about **3.2 m**
Each piece plus one saw cut, divided into the length; round **down**
6 000 mm cut into 890 mm pieces with 3 mm cuts: 6 000 ÷ 893 = 6.7, so **6 pieces**
30 joints at 4 a day: 7.5, so **8 days**
Mass per joint × joints, then whole packs; round **up**
34 joints × 0.35 kg = 11.9 kg; in 5 kg packs: **3 packs**

blocks.note: Round in the direction that is safe for the job: you cannot cut 6.7 pieces, so round down; you cannot finish in 7.5 days, so round up. Work every sum twice, the second time a different way if you can.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Measure the spool against the isometric and check flange faces are square and bolt holes two-holed.
Clear all slag, spatter, rods, rags and tools out of the bore and check it with a torch: debris left inside damages pumps and valves.
Cap the pipe ends and cover flange faces to protect the bevels and machined faces.
Hand in the weld log, inspection records and NDT reports; report the weld count, repairs and anything outside the WPS to your supervisor.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what the WPS, PQR and WPQ are and check that a WPS covers a joint.
I can say which positions a 1G, 2G, 5G, 6G or 6GR pipe test generally covers, and check a welder's qualification before giving out work.
I can read nominal pipe size and schedule, and work out a bore from the OD and wall.
I can name the common butt-weld fittings and flanges and say how each is welded.
I can work out a cut length from an isometric drawing, allowing for fittings and root gaps.
I can control the hazards of pipe work, including rolling pipe, trenches, fuel lines and radiography.
I can explain why E6010 is used for the root and E7018 for the fill and cap, and store each correctly.
I can prepare, bevel, clean, fit up and tack a pipe joint to the WPS.
I can run an open root with a keyhole and a whip and pause, and correct it as I go round the pipe.
I can run a hot pass and clean between passes to remove wagon tracks and slag.
I can weld fill and cap passes in the 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G positions.
I can name pipe weld defects, their causes and cures, and record them with clock positions.
I can explain how bend test strips are taken, prepared, bent and judged.
I can explain radiography, hydrostatic testing and the repair of a rejected weld.
I can plan a pipe job, do the calculations and keep a weld log.

terms: American Welding Society; its codes set rules for procedures, welders and inspection
The angled face ground or cut on a pipe end to make the groove
A small piece welded across the outside of a joint to hold it, so the root runs clear
The final pass on the outside of the joint
A list of pipe pieces to cut, with their lengths and identification
A pass between the hot pass and the cap that builds up the groove
Misalignment between the inside walls of two pipe ends
The pass run soon after the root, at higher current, to burn out slag and strengthen the root
A single-line 3-D pipe drawing showing the route, fittings, dimensions and weld numbers
The small hole at the front of the root pool that shows the root faces are melting through
An elbow whose centre-line radius is 1.5 × the nominal size
A root welded with a gap and no backing
Testing with X-rays or gamma rays to see inside a weld
The flat land left at the bottom of the bevel
The space between the pipe ends at the root before welding
The number that sets a pipe's wall thickness
A bend test strip turned on its side, used on thick walls
A section of pipe with its fittings, made in the shop
Setting flange bolt holes to straddle the centre lines
Slag lines along both edges of a pipe root
The record of each weld: number, welder, materials, passes, inspection and repairs
A flange with a long tapered hub, butt welded to the pipe
The root motion: flick forward to let the pool freeze, come back and hold to fill
Welder performance qualification: proof a welder passed a test, and what it covers
Welding procedure specification: the written method for making a weld

c1.title: A chilled-water line for a hotel in Negril
c1.text: Dwayne leads a crew installing an NPS 6 schedule 40 carbon steel chilled-water line in a hotel plant room in Negril, Westmoreland. Most joints are fixed horizontal (5G), welded uphill with an E6010 root and E7018 fill and cap to the WPS. Marlon's welder qualification is for a 2G test on NPS 2 schedule 80 pipe. Tanisha holds a 6G test on NPS 6 schedule 80 pipe.

c2.title: A pump-house spool in Spanish Town
c2.text: A shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine, is building an NPS 4 schedule 40 spool for a pump house. The isometric gives 900 mm from the face of a weld neck flange to the centre of a 90° long-radius elbow. The flange table gives 76 mm through the hub, the elbow is 152 mm centre to end, and the WPS root gap is 3 mm. A small-bore drain will be socket welded to the spool, and the client plans to pressure test the finished spool.

c3.title: A tie-in on a water main near Bog Walk
c3.text: Shawn's crew must weld a new NPS 8 branch into an existing carbon steel water main beside the road near Bog Walk, St Catherine. The main is in service. Work starts at 6:30 a.m., when the pipe is wet with dew. The new pipe was unloaded with a lifting magnet, and on the first joint near the open end of the new run the root arc keeps swinging to one side.

c4.title: Practice coupons at a training centre in Papine
c4.text: At a training centre in Papine, St Andrew, a group is practising 2G pipe coupons with an E6010 root and E7018 stringers. Two coupons are being prepared for bend tests, and a licensed radiographer is booked for the afternoon to shoot three other coupons in the yard beside the welding bays.

c5.title: A fire main at a warehouse in Portmore
c5.text: Kadeen is team leader on a new NPS 4 schedule 40 fire main at a warehouse in Portmore. The line has 34 butt joints. Each joint uses about 0.35 kg of E7018, which the store sells in 5 kg sealed packs. On one joint, the root came out with a high hump down the middle and deep grooves on both edges, and on another the finished cap leaves the bevel edges showing at 3 o'clock.

questions.q: The first joints Dwayne must give out are fixed 5G joints. Which statement about Marlon is correct?
o: His 2G test does not cover the vertical and overhead parts of a 5G joint
His test covers every position, because a pipe test always covers all positions
He can weld them if Tanisha welds the root and he welds only the cap
He can weld them because his test was on a thicker schedule 80 wall
questions.why: A 2G pipe test generally covers only the flat and horizontal positions. A fixed 5G joint needs the vertical and overhead positions, so the welder needs a 5G or 6G test (or 2G plus 5G) that covers them.

questions.q: Inside Tanisha's root, the bead is hollow below the bore surface between 5 and 7 o'clock. What should she change on the next root?
o: Raise the current so the bottom of the root sinks in deeper
Push the electrode well into the gap and keep a tight arc
Open the root gap wider at the bottom of the joint only
Weld that part of the root downhill so it freezes faster
questions.why: Concavity (suck-back) happens in the overhead part of a fixed joint, where gravity pulls the pool back from the inside. Pushing the electrode into the gap with a tight arc and a small keyhole forces metal up to the bore surface.

questions.q: Tanisha asks for a remote current control at each joint. Why is it useful on a 5G root?
o: It lets her switch from DC to AC when the arc starts to wander
It stops the electrode sticking when she strikes on a cold tack
It lets her lower the current as the pipe heats near the top
It keeps the open-circuit voltage low so she cannot get a shock
questions.why: As the root climbs the pipe, the joint heats up and the keyhole tends to grow, giving excess penetration and icicles near the top. A remote control lets the welder trim the current at the joint without leaving it.

questions.q: When the line-up clamp is taken off one joint, a tack at 10 o'clock cracks. What should Dwayne tell the welder to do?
o: Weld the root over it slowly, so the heat closes the crack
Leave it and put an extra tack beside it to hold the gap
Run a short fillet over the outside of the cracked tack
Grind it out completely and re-tack before the root
questions.why: A crack in a tack stays in the root if it is welded over, and can grow in service. The tack is ground out completely, the gap and alignment are checked, and the joint is re-tacked.

questions.q: What is the cut length of the pipe between the flange and the elbow?
o: 666 mm
672 mm
669 mm
742 mm
questions.why: Take off the flange (76 mm), the elbow (152 mm) and the two root gaps (3 mm each): 900 − 76 − 152 − 6 = 666 mm. Forgetting the gaps gives 672 mm; forgetting the flange gives 742 mm.

questions.q: After the root on the flange joint, the flange face has pulled out of square towards 12 o'clock. What should the welder do next?
o: Weld the next passes starting at 12 o'clock, where the joint is already hot
Weld the next pass on the 6 o'clock side first, then re-check the face
Cut the flange off at once and fit a new one before going on
Carry on round as normal; the cap will pull the face back square
questions.why: Shrinkage pulls the face towards the side that was welded. Welding the opposite side next uses that shrinkage to pull it back. Check the face with a flange square after each pass, and weld in a balanced order from the start.

questions.q: The client asks to test the spool with compressed air, because it is quicker than filling it with water. Why do most codes prefer water?
o: Air leaves moisture in the pipe that rusts the welds
Air cannot reach the test pressure in a closed spool
Compressed air stores far more energy and can burst violently
Water finds the leaks because it turns the welds a different colour
questions.why: Water hardly compresses, so if a weld fails the pressure falls at once. Compressed air stores a great deal of energy, and a failure can throw pieces of pipe. That is why hydrostatic testing is the usual choice.

questions.q: The fitter pushes the drain pipe right to the bottom of its socket-weld fitting and tacks it. What is wrong?
o: The pipe should have been bevelled before it went in
Socket welds must be tacked inside the bore, not outside
The fitting must be heated so it expands over the pipe
It should be pulled back about 1.5 mm before tacking
questions.why: The small gap at the bottom of the socket lets the pipe expand as it is welded. Without it, the shrinking fillet pulls against a pipe that cannot move, and the weld can crack at its root.

questions.q: Before anyone cuts into the existing main, what must Shawn have confirmed?
o: That the main is isolated, drained and made safe under a permit
That the water in the main is cold enough to cool the cut
That the new branch has been fully welded and radiographed first
That the road traffic has stopped for the whole of the day
questions.why: Cutting into a line under pressure, or one that still holds water, can injure the crew and flood the trench. The owner isolates and drains it, the crew confirm it is safe, and the work runs under the site's permit.

questions.q: The pipe is wet with dew when the crew is ready to weld. What should be done?
o: Weld at once with a higher current, which dries the joint as it goes
Warm the joint area gently until it is dry, as the WPS asks
Wipe it with an oily rag so the water runs off the bevels
Change to E6010 for every pass, because it does not mind water
questions.why: Water on the joint brings hydrogen and porosity into the weld, especially under E7018. Warming the joint area until the metal is dry (and at least at the WPS minimum preheat) removes it before welding.

questions.q: The root arc near the open end of the new run keeps being pushed to one side. Which action should the welder try first?
o: Turn the current up so the arc is too strong to be pushed
Hold a longer arc so the arc has room to swing back
Move the work clamp or wrap the lead round the pipe
Strike the arc on the outside of the pipe and drag it into the gap
questions.why: This is arc blow: magnetism in the pipe, made worse by the lifting magnet and the open end, pushes a DC arc aside. Changing where the current enters the pipe, a shorter arc and welding towards a heavy tack all reduce it.

questions.q: A face bend from one 2G coupon opens along a line of slag between two cap stringers. What should that trainee change?
o: Use one wide weave for the cap instead of separate stringers
Raise the current on the root pass and on the hot pass
Bend the next strip round a larger former in the jig
Clean each stringer fully and overlap each bead about half
questions.why: Slag between stringers comes from poor cleaning and beads that do not overlap enough, leaving a slot where slag sits. Brushing every stringer and overlapping each bead by about half gives a sound, fused cap.

questions.q: Why are the cap and root ground flush with the pipe before the strips are bent?
o: So the strip bends evenly and the test stretches the weld itself
So the inspector can read the welder's stamp on the face of the strip
So the strip fits between the jaws of the band saw for cutting
So the strip is light enough for one person to bend by hand
questions.why: Reinforcement left on a strip makes the strain gather at its toes, so the strip may crack there for the wrong reason. Ground flush, with the marks running lengthways, the whole weld is stretched fairly.

questions.q: The radiographer sets up a barrier round the yard while trainees are still welding in the bays beside it. What should happen?
o: Carry on welding behind the bay screens, which stop the rays
Stop work and move out of the controlled area until it is cleared
Carry on, as long as everyone keeps their helmets down
Ask the radiographer to work faster so the welding is not held up
questions.why: Welding screens and helmets do not stop X-rays or gamma rays. Everyone leaves the controlled area when the radiographer says and stays out until it is declared clear.

questions.q: How many 5 kg packs of E7018 should Kadeen order for the joints?
o: 2 packs
12 packs
3 packs
6 packs
questions.why: 34 × 0.35 kg = 11.9 kg. Two packs (10 kg) are not enough, so round up to 3 packs (15 kg). Ordering 12 packs mistakes kilograms for packs.

questions.q: What should be done to the root with the high hump and deep edge grooves before the hot pass?
o: Run the hot pass at a lower current so it does not burn through
Leave it, as the fill passes will cover the hump
Weld a second root pass over it from inside the pipe
Grind the hump down and open the grooves, then run the hot pass
questions.why: The deep grooves are wagon tracks full of slag, and the hump would make the hot pass ride over them and trap it. Grinding flattens the root and opens the tracks, so the hot pass can melt in and fuse the edges.

questions.q: On the other joint the cap leaves the bevel edges showing at 3 o'clock. What is this fault and what is the cure?
o: Underfill: add weld to fill the groove and lap the edges
Undercut: grind the whole cap down level with the pipe surface
Overlap: grind the extra metal off the pipe surface beside it
Excess penetration: grind the root flush from inside the bore
questions.why: When the cap does not reach the pipe surface, the joint is underfilled and thinner than the pipe wall. More weld is added, lapping about 1.5 mm past each bevel edge, then the area is cleaned and re-inspected.

questions.q: A store has two lengths of NPS 4 pipe, one schedule 40 and one schedule 80. Which statement is true?
o: The schedule 80 pipe has the larger outside diameter of the two
Same outside diameter; the schedule 80 pipe has the smaller bore
Same bore; the schedule 80 pipe has the larger outside diameter
The schedule 40 pipe has the thicker wall and so the smaller bore
questions.why: For a given nominal size the outside diameter stays the same, so the same fittings fit. A higher schedule means a thicker wall, which is taken from the inside: schedule 80 NPS 4 has a 8.56 mm wall against 6.02 mm.

questions.q: A designer chooses long-radius elbows for a water line wherever there is room. Why?
o: They are lighter, so the line needs fewer pipe supports
They need no root gap, so fit-up is quicker
Their gentler bend gives smoother flow and less wear
They are the only elbows that can be radiographed
questions.why: A long-radius elbow (radius 1.5 × NPS) turns the flow more gently than a short-radius one, so pressure loss and erosion are lower. Short-radius elbows are used only where space is tight.

questions.q: Why are the far ends of a pipe run capped or plugged while the root is welded on site?
o: To stop the root gap closing up as the pipe cools down
To keep the radiographer's film dry inside the pipe
To hold the pipe still so that it cannot roll
To stop a draught through the bore cooling the root
questions.why: Wind through an open pipe acts like a chimney: it cools the root and blows the gas shield away inside, causing porosity on the inside of the root. Capping the ends and screening the joint keeps the bore still.
